chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub narrated from Ahmad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Khalid ibn Jarir, from Abu al-Rabii, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who has money in his hand for his orphan brother, and he is his executor/will-trustee. Is it suitable for him to trade with it? He said: 'Yes, he trades with it as he trades with the money of others, and the profit is shared between them.' I said: 'Is there guarantee/liability on him?' He said: 'No, if he is managing it (for the benefit of the orphan).'

As for the profit, it belongs to the orphan whenever the manager transacts with it, and the manager does not currently have enough to cover that money. So when the matter is as we mentioned, he is liable for the capital, the profit belongs to the orphan, and the zakat is on the orphan's money, and it is the responsibility of the guardian to pay it from it, provided he did not intend by the trade merely to manage it for the orphan. This is the category we mentioned earlier and for which we have narrated many reports.

And whenever his intention is to manage it for the orphan, it is permissible for him to take from the profit an amount that serves as his livelihood (sufficiency). This is the meaning of the preceding report: 'the profit is shared between them.'
And whenever the trader with the orphan's money is capable (of having his own money) in the current state, then liability is upon him, the profit belongs to him, and the zakat is upon him.
And that which indicates this is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: What are the rules for profit, liability, and zakat when a guardian trades with an orphan's money?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) delineates the fiduciary principles for managing an orphan's wealth, distinguishing between a guardian who trades with the orphan's funds due to lack of personal capital and one who is financially self-sufficient. In the former case, the guardian assumes liability for the capital while profits are shared, whereas in the latter, he bears full liability, retains the profit, and is responsible for zakat. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the guardian's intent and financial status in determining risk allocation and entitlement to earnings from the orphan's assets.
